judgements.title: LLM01: Prompt Injection
judgements.evidence: REVIEW_SECONDS_PER_FILE: int = 300  # the review's own budget, files times this, under the ceiling; 0 leaves only the ceiling

judges.reason: The quoted line is a plain explanatory comment about a seconds-per-file budget; it contains no imperative or instruction to any model, so the claim that it holds text meant to steer an LLM is false.
The quoted line is an ordinary configuration comment about a timeout budget; it contains no instruction addressed to a model, so there is nothing to remove as injection.

The comment carries what the name cannot: the budget is files times this value, it is capped by REVIEW_TIMEOUT_SECONDS, and 0 disables it, so deleting it loses semantics, not verbosity.

judgements.title: SQL Injection via f-string interpolation in dynamic DDL generation
judgements.evidence: ddl = (f"CREATE {'UNIQUE ' if index.unique else ''}INDEX IF NOT EXISTS {quote(index.name)} "

judges.reason: Every identifier interpolated comes from Base.metadata (table.name, index.name, index.columns) or the inspector, each passed through dialect.identifier_preparer.quote; SQL identifiers cannot be bind parameters, so the suggested text() fix is impossible and there is no user-controlled input on this path.

Every interpolated identifier comes from Base.metadata.sorted_tables and table.indexes and goes through dialect.identifier_preparer.quote; no request or user value reaches the DDL, and text() cannot bind identifiers anyway.

judgements.title: Database URL passed directly to export without validation risks SSRF or connection hijacking
judgements.evidence: count = asyncio.run(export(args.database, args.out, args.repository, args.older_than))

judges.reason: --database is a SQLAlchemy URL typed by the operator running the script locally (default: the app's own DATABASE_URL); it is a connection the operator chooses, not attacker-supplied input, so there is no SSRF surface to validate.
--database is the operator's own command-line override of DATABASE_URL in a script they invoke from a shell; there is no remote input to the argument, so no SSRF or hijack path exists to close.

judgements.title: Unvalidated file path for output allows arbitrary file writes
judgements.evidence: count = asyncio.run(export(args.database, args.out, args.repository, args.older_than))

judges.reason: export_reviews.py is an operator-run maintenance CLI whose whole purpose is writing to the --out path the operator names; there is no trust boundary to confine it to, and the caller already has the shell's filesystem rights.

args.out comes from argparse in a local admin script run as `python scripts/export_reviews.py` by the operator; a path check would only stop the operator writing where they asked, with no trust boundary crossed.

judgements.title: Broad exception handler masks critical errors in a long-running service
judgements.evidence: except Exception as e:  # noqa: BLE001

judges.reason: The finding's own concrete ask is already in the code: 'except asyncio.CancelledError: raise' sits on lines 49-50 immediately above, and the remaining breadth is deliberate, marked # noqa: BLE001 and documented in the docstring as 'it never stops the loop'.

Nothing is masked: asyncio.CancelledError is re-raised at lines 49-50, the rest is logged at error level, and the broad catch with `# noqa: BLE001` is what keeps the nightly loop alive, as the docstring states.

judgements.title: swallowed_exception_details
judgements.evidence: logger.error("retention sweep failed", error=type(e).__name__)

judges.reason: The handler logs only type(e).__name__, so an unattended daily sweep loses both the exception message and the traceback; for the loop's only observability that is a one-word change to logger.exception a maintainer would take.

error=type(e).__name__ is the house convention at some fifteen call sites and logger.exception appears nowhere; the one place the message is used it is redacted first (review_runner.py:401), matching the README rule that logs carry no code.

judgements.title: yagni, delete hardcoded test fixture object
judgements.evidence: FINDING = {"path": "a.py", "line": 2, "category": "security", "severity": "high", "title": "t", "evidence": "e", "recommendation": "r", "confidence": 0.9}

judges.reason: A fixed FINDING dict is what makes the retention assertions deterministic; the recommendation to generate random titles, categories and severities would weaken the test rather than fix a defect.

FINDING is a minimal literal fixture for a retention sweep that never inspects its fields; swapping it for randomised factory data would make the test nondeterministic, so the advice would be rejected.

judgements.title: A05:2025 - Injection of secrets via environment variable manipulation
judgements.evidence: _PLACEHOLDERS = {"GITHUB_APP_ID": "0", "GITHUB_PRIVATE_KEY": "", "GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET": "x" * 32,

judges.reason: The placeholders exist so config.settings can be imported at all, and the module docstring plus render() show the table is read from the class, never an instance, with secrets rendered as 'required' (asserted by test_settings_reference.py); no placeholder can reach the output.

The placeholders are the defence: the script seeds fake secrets and pops the fatal names so config.settings can be imported without any real secret, and render() reads cls.model_fields, never an instance's values.

judgements.title: YAGNI: Remove redundant assertion message text
judgements.evidence: assert short == [], "a description shorter than a sentence is a label, not a description"

judges.reason: The assertion message states the rule the test enforces (a sub-30-character description is a label, not a description), which is the information a failing CI line needs; removing it costs diagnosis and fixes nothing.

The assertion message states the rule being enforced (a description under 30 characters is a label); deleting a pytest message that explains a failing assertion is a preference and makes the failure harder to read.

judgements.title: YAGNI: Remove redundant assertion message text
judgements.evidence: assert REFERENCE.read_text(encoding="utf-8") == rendered, ("docs/SETTINGS.md is stale: cd backend && .venv/bin/python scripts/settings_reference.py > ../docs/SETTINGS.md")

judges.reason: The message is the regeneration command for a staleness check, the single most useful thing to print when docs/SETTINGS.md drifts; deleting it makes the failure harder to act on.
The message is the regenerate command for a stale docs/SETTINGS.md, which is exactly what the reader of the failure needs; removing it costs the fix instruction and repairs no defect.

judgements.title: YAGNI: Remove unnecessary path manipulation for local imports
judgements.evidence: sys.path.insert(0, str(Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1] / "scripts"))

judges.reason: Inserting backend/scripts on sys.path is the ordinary way to import a script that is not a package, and the suggested importlib.import_module('settings_reference', package='backend.scripts') would not resolve it; nothing is broken here.

The sys.path insert is required, not unnecessary: backend/scripts has no __init__.py, so settings_reference is not importable as a module and the suggested importlib.import_module('settings_reference', package='backend.scripts') would fail.
